The wins of a prominent coach were vacated down from 409 to 298 as part of the initial consent decree signed between a major university and the NCAA, as well as a single win by an interim coach at another institution, which I never understood because that win occurred after the head coach was fired. 

Later, state legislators challenged the NCAA's ability to move $60 million in fine money earmarked for child protection charities outside of the state where those funds were generated (a state where a convicted abuser was allowed to adopt children, including one away from his biological parents and where we later learned there was a significant pedophilia ring within the clergy). 

The NCAA denied the legislators' request to allow the money to stay in the state, leading the legislators to file a lawsuit. During the discovery process, it was revealed that the NCAA was involved in the independent report that led to the university sanctions, and the NCAA settled the lawsuit instead of having further internal documents revealed, backing off most of the sanctions, and allowing the money to remain in the state, as well as restoring the coach's wins. 

I would add that, in my opinion, vacating wins is a paper punishment and I haven't ever seen evidence to suggest that style of punishment is a deterrent to breaking rules. In this case specifically, it ended up being a punishment to living players and didn't have an effect on a deceased man.
